history.answer: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter born in 1907 and active between 1925 and 1954[3]. She is recognized for her many portraits, self-portraits, and works inspired by the nature and artifacts of Mexico[1]. Kahlo is also described as a surrealist or magical realist[1][5], and she is known for painting about her experience of chronic pain[1]. Her work made her a symbol of Mexican culture, feminism, and LGBT culture[2]. Furthermore, her personal life and artwork were heavily influenced by the Mexicanidad movement, which aimed to revitalize the culture of Mexico's indigenous peoples[2]. Kahlo used self-portraits therapeutically to project her anguish and pain, and scholars interpret these self-portraits as a method for her to reclaim her body from medical issues and gender conformity by using her own image against patriarchal tradition[3]. She was born in the house where she spent her childhood, which remained her family home throughout her life[4].

Kahlo and Rivera were married in a civil ceremony at the town hall of Coyoacán on 21 August 1929. Her mother opposed the marriage, and both parents referred to it as a "marriage between an elephant and a dove", referring to the couple's differences in size; Rivera was tall and overweight while Kahlo was petite and fragile. Regardless, her father approved of Rivera, who was wealthy and therefore able to support Kahlo, who could not work and had to receive expensive medical treatment. The wedding was reported by the Mexican and international press, and the marriage was subject to constant media attention in Mexico in the following years, with articles referring to the couple as simply "Diego and Frida".

The Amazon basin is the most biodiverse region in the world, being home to many of the Earth's plant, mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian, fish and insect species. While being very biodiverse the majority of the Amazon basin is sparsely populated by humans with the exceptions of cities such as Manaus and Belém. There are many indigenous communities who represent many different cultures and languages. For the people living in the Amazon basin fishing and agriculture are a very important livelihood.

The Statue of Liberty, also known as *Liberty Enlightening the World*, is a colossal neoclassical sculpture of a robed and crowned woman located on Liberty Island in New York Harbor[1][2]. It was dedicated on October 28, 1886[1].

Key details about the statue include:
*   It is a figure of a classically draped woman inspired by the Roman goddess of liberty, Libertas[1].
*   The creator of the statue is Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, along with Richard Morris Hunt and Gustave Eiffel[5].
*   The monument includes Liberty Island and Ellis Island, which together form the Statue of Liberty National Monument[2].

After its unveiling in 1886, the statue became an iconic symbol of American freedom, frequently appearing on posters, postcards, pictures, and books[3]. It is recognized as a popular and recognizable local, national, and international icon and political symbol, often being the first significant item seen by arriving immigrants[3].

The Statue of Liberty (Liberty Enlightening the World; ) is a colossal neoclassical sculpture of a robed and crowned woman on Liberty Island, part of New York City, in New York Harbor. The copper-clad statue, a gift to the United States from the people of France, was designed by French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, and its metal framework built by Gustave Eiffel. The statue was dedicated on October 28, 1886.
The statue is a figure of a classically draped woman, inspired by the Roman goddess of liberty, Libertas. She holds a torch above her head with her right hand, and in her left hand carries a tabula ansata inscribed JULY IV MDCCLXXVI (July 4, 1776, in Roman numerals), the date of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. With her left foot she steps on a broken chain and shackle, commemorating the national abolition of slavery following the American Civil War.

top.text:
Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor. He is known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system.
Born and raised in the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Tesla first studied engineering and physics in the 1870s without receiving a degree. He then gained practical experience in the early 1880s working in telephony and at Continental Edison in the new electric power industry. In 1884, he migrated to the United States, where he became a naturalized citizen. He worked for a short time at the Edison Machine Works in New York City before he struck out on his own. With the help of partners to finance and market his ideas, Tesla set up laboratories and companies in New York to develop a range of electrical and mechanical devices. His AC induction motor and related polyphase AC patents, licensed by Westinghouse Electric in 1888, earned him a considerable amount of money and became the cornerstone of the polyphase system, which Westinghouse marketed.

Mount Kibo is its highest point, with an elevation of 5,895 m (19,340 ft) above sea level[6]. While Mount Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa, it has three peaks: Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira, with Kibo being the tallest peak[4][6]. Mount Kenya is noted as the second highest mountain in Africa[4].

top.text:
Mount Kilimanjaro () is a large dormant volcano in Tanzania. It is the highest mountain in Africa and the highest free-standing mountain above sea level in the world, at 5,895 m (19,340 ft) above sea level and 4900 m (16,000 ft) above its plateau base. It is also the highest volcano in the Eastern Hemisphere and the fourth most prominent peak on Earth.
Kilimanjaro's southern and eastern slopes served as the home of the Chagga Kingdoms until their abolition in 1963 by Julius Nyerere. The origin and meaning of the name Kilimanjaro is unknown, but may mean "mountain of greatness" or "unclimbable". Although it is described in classical sources, German missionary Johannes Rebmann is credited as the first European to report the mountain's existence, in 1848. After several European attempts, Hans Meyer reached Kilimanjaro's highest summit in 1889.

Insulin is a peptide hormone that is produced by the beta cells in the pancreatic islets and is encoded in humans by the insulin (INS) gene[1]. It has a molecular mass of 5808 Da[3] or 5805.6444 Da[5].

Insulin functions by strongly inhibiting glucose production and secretion by the liver when its concentration in the blood is high[1]. Furthermore, circulating insulin influences the synthesis of proteins across many different tissues[1]. Conversely, low levels of insulin in the blood promote widespread catabolism, particularly of reserve body fat[1].

There are three main types of insulin medication: short-acting (like regular insulin), intermediate-acting (such as neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin), and longer-acting (like insulin glargine)[2]. While human insulin is a specific molecule, insulin from non-human animal sources can differ in effectiveness regarding carbohydrate metabolism effects compared to human insulin[3]. Historically, Frederick Banting and Charles Best first isolated insulin from the dog pancreas in 1921[4].

Tides are the regular rise and fall in water level observed in oceans and seas, which are primarily caused by the gravitational tidal forces exerted by the Moon upon the Earth[1]. These tides are also significantly influenced by the Sun's tidal forces, the Earth's rotation, and the shape of rocky continents that can block the flow of oceanic water[1][2].

During each tidal cycle, water at any specific location reaches a maximum height called "high tide" before receding to a minimum level known as "low tide"[2]. As the water ebbs, it exposes more of the foreshore, which is referred to as the intertidal zone[2][3]. These tidal forces also cause changes in the depth of marine and estuarine water bodies and generate oscillating currents called tidal streams[3]. Furthermore, the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun causes the displacement of the solid Earth's surface, known as earth tides or terrestrial tides[4].

Tides are the periodic rise and fall of sea level caused by the differential gravitational forces exerted primarily by the Moon and the Sun, combined with inertial effects from the Earth–Moon system's orbital motion[1]. These astronomical forcings create tidal potential, which results in corresponding motions or currents in the world's oceans as the Earth rotates[2].

Specifically, the primary effect of lunar tidal forces is to cause two bulges in the Earth's oceans: one on the side facing the Moon and another on the opposite side[5]. Because the Earth rotates on its axis, one of these ocean bulges (high tide) remains positioned "under" the Moon, while a corresponding tide occurs on the opposite side[5]. The timing of tides varies widely across the Earth due to continental boundaries[4]. Furthermore, actual observed tides are modified by terrestrial factors such as the geometry of ocean basins, continental boundaries, bathymetry, and the Coriolis effect[1]. Ocean tides are cyclic, rising and falling approximately twice a day, with four stages in the cycle including reaching a local minimum called low tide[3].

The Cold War was a period of geopolitical tension between the United States and the Soviet Union and their respective allies, the capitalist Western Bloc and the communist Eastern Bloc[3][4]. This tension began following World War II in 1945[4]. The term "cold war" is used because there was no direct fighting between the two superpowers[1][3][4], but they each supported opposing sides in regional conflicts known as proxy wars[1][3][4].

This state of conflict involved political actions, economic and military competition, propaganda, acts of espionage, and sports diplomacy[1][2]. Specific examples of this competition included technological competitions like the Space Race[4] and the continued political conflict, military tension, and economic competition between the Soviet Union and its satellite states and the powers of the Western world led by the United States from 1945 to 1991[5].

Plants grow through primary growth, which occurs from the tips of roots or shoots and results in the lengthening of roots and stems, setting the foundation for organ formation[2]. This process is influenced by the interaction between a plant's genome and its physical and biotic environment[3].

The growth of plants involves several aspects:
*   **Reproduction:** Plants can reproduce asexually by growing structures that can develop into new plants, such as mosses or liverworts breaking into pieces to regrow[1]. Some non-flowering plants, like many liverworts, mosses, and some clubmosses, also grow by producing gemmae cells that can detach and grow[1].
*   **Organ Systems:** Vascular plants possess two main organ systems: a shoot system and a root system[4]. The root system is typically underground, serving to anchor the plant, absorb water and minerals, store carbohydrates, and transport nutrients like sugar and oxygen to other organs such as the xyleme and phloeme[4].
*   **Growth Habit:** Tree growth habits are an evolutionary adaptation where plants grow taller to better compete for sunlight[5]. Trees often become tall and long-lived, with some reaching several thousand years old[5]. They develop modified structures like thicker stems made of specialized cells that provide structural strength and durability, allowing them to grow taller and spread their foliage[5].

Plants can also tolerate stresses like frost and dehydration by having protective mechanisms such as antifreeze proteins, heat-shock proteins, and sugars in their cytoplasm[3].

Plants grow by obtaining energy from sunlight through photosynthesis, which is done using a green pigment[1]. Plants are eukaryotic organisms that belong to the kingdom Plantae[1].

Growth involves various forms and life cycles:
*   **Life Cycles:** Most herbaceous plants have a perennial life cycle (85%), while some are annual (15%) or biennial (<1%)[3]. Annual plants complete their entire life cycle, from germination to seed production, within one growing season before dying[5].
*   **Growth Forms:** Plants exhibit diverse growth habits. For example, the Fabaceae family has a wide variety of forms, including trees, shrubs, herbaceous plants, and vines or lianas[4]. Herbaceous plants can be annuals, biennials, or perennials without having basal or terminal leaf aggregations[4].
*   **Vine Growth:** Certain plants always grow as vines, while others may only grow as vines part of the time. Vines can use supports like rock exposures or other plants to reach sunlight with minimal energy investment in supportive tissue[2]. Some legumes have tendrils[4], and vines support themselves by twisting shoots around a support or through tendrils[4].
*   **Plant Types:** Plants can be classified as heliophytes, mesophytes, or xerophytes depending on their environmental needs[4].

Plants are the eukaryotic organisms that constitute the kingdom Plantae . They are predominantly photosynthetic or came from photosynthetic ancestors, meaning that they obtain their energy from sunlight by using the green pigment chlorophyll in their chloroplasts to produce sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Over the course of time, some plants have evolved to be parasitic, meaning they take energy from other organisms. Except for glaucophytes, some green algae and a few red algae, most plants are multicellular.
Historically, as in Aristotle's biology, the plant kingdom encompassed all living things that were not animals, and included algae and fungi. Definitions have narrowed since then; current definitions exclude fungi and some of the algae. By the definition used in this article, plants form the clade Viridiplantae (green plants), which consists of the green algae and the embryophytes or land plants (hornworts, liverworts, mosses, lycophytes, ferns, conifers and other gymnosperms, and flowering plants). A definition based on genomes includes the Viridiplantae, along with the red algae and the glaucophytes, in the clade Archaeplastida.

DNA, or deoxyribonucleic acid, is a molecule that carries most of the genetic instructions necessary for the growth, development, functioning, and reproduction of all known living organisms and many viruses[2]. It is a nucleic acid, along with proteins and complex carbohydrates, one of the three major macromolecules essential for all known life forms[2].

DNA has a double-stranded structure where two polynucleotide chains coil around each other to form a characteristic double helix[1][4]. Each single strand of DNA is made up of nucleotides, which consist of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and a nucleobase[4]. These nucleotides link together via phosphodiester bonds to create the phosphate-deoxyribose backbone of the double helix, with the nucleobases pointing toward the opposing strand[4]. In DNA, the pyrimidines are thymine and cytosine, while the purines are adenine and guanine[1]. The segments of DNA that carry genetic information are called genes[3], and other sequences serve structural purposes or regulate the use of this information[3].

DNA, or deoxyribonucleic acid, is a macromolecule that carries most of the genetic instructions for the growth, development, functioning, and reproduction of all known living organisms and many viruses[1]. It is composed of nucleotide units linked by covalent bonds and hydrogen bonds in a repeating structure[1]. These nucleotides consist of a deoxyribose sugar molecule, a phosphate group, and a base (amine group), which together form a nucleotide that links to create long DNA chains[2]. Genetic information is stored in the sequence of these nucleotides, and genes are stretches of this sequence along the DNA chain[2].

DNA exists in a double-stranded form where two complementary strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between the nitrogenous bases (A with T, and C with G)[3][4]. Within cells, DNA is organized into long structures called chromosomes[3]. During cell division, DNA replication occurs, which makes exact copies of the DNA so that each newly divided daughter cell receives its own complete set of chromosomes[3][4]. Eukaryotes typically store most of their DNA inside the cell nucleus[3].

DNA exists in many possible conformations that include A-DNA, B-DNA, and Z-DNA forms, although only B-DNA and Z-DNA have been directly observed in functional organisms. The conformation that DNA adopts depends on the hydration level, DNA sequence, the amount and direction of supercoiling, chemical modifications of the bases, the type and concentration of metal ions, and the presence of polyamines in solution.
The first published reports of A-DNA X-ray diffraction patterns—and also B-DNA—used analyses based on Patterson functions that provided only a limited amount of structural information for oriented fibers of DNA. An alternative analysis was proposed by Wilkins et al. in 1953 for the in vivo B-DNA X-ray diffraction-scattering patterns of highly hydrated DNA fibers in terms of squares of Bessel functions. In the same journal, James Watson and Francis Crick presented their molecular modeling analysis of the DNA X-ray diffraction patterns to suggest that the structure was a double helix.

The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes that operated from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century[1]. It is considered a Eurasian trade route that played a significant role in global communication and interaction[3].

The name "Silk Road" originates from the valuable trade in silk, which first developed in China, leading to an extensive transcontinental network of trade routes[2]. This term comes from the German word *Seidenstraße* (literally "Silk Road")[2]. While maritime commerce connected areas like the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean worlds, overland trade across Central Asia also expanded during antiquity[4]. During the Roman Empire, the Silk Road became the main overland trade network linking East Asia with the Mediterranean[4]. Some historians suggest that this route was fundamental to the cultural unity of the Afro-Eurasian world[3].

The Silk Road was an ancient network of trade routes connecting communities across Eurasia by both land and sea, stretching from the Mediterranean basin in the west to the Korean peninsula and the Japanese archipelago in the east[4]. This route saw immense political variation over time, influenced by events such as the Mongol conquests and the Black Death[1].

The Silk Road was a significant factor in the development of various civilizations, including China, India, Ancient Egypt, Persia, Arabia, and Ancient Rome[2]. Over centuries, while some dynasties prospered or perished, the route linking Europe and Asia survived and expanded, which is why it is still known as the Silk Road today[2]. Furthermore, diseases like the plague spread along this route, possibly contributing to the Black Death[1]. In the 21st century, the term "New Silk Road" is used for large infrastructure projects along historic trade routes, such as the Eurasian Land Bridge and the Chinese Belt and Road Initiative (BRI)[3].

top.text: The Silk Road was utilized over a period that saw immense political variation across the continent, exemplified by major events such as the Black Death and the Mongol conquests. The network was highly decentralized, and security was sparse: travelers faced constant threats of banditry and nomadic raiders, and long expanses of inhospitable terrain. Few individuals traveled the entire length of the Silk Road, instead relying on a succession of middlemen based at various stopping points along the way. In addition to goods, the network facilitated an unprecedented exchange of religious (especially Buddhist), philosophical, and scientific thought, much of which was syncretised by societies along the way. Likewise, a wide variety of people used the routes. Diseases such as plague also spread along the Silk Road, possibly contributing to the Black Death.

A dolphin is any of the 40 extant species of aquatic mammal belonging to various cetacean families[1]. The term "dolphin" can refer to most species in the family Delphinidae (oceanic dolphins) and several river dolphin families, including Iniidae (South American river dolphins), Pontoporiidae, Lipotidae, and Platanistidae[3]. Casually, the name is also used as a synonym for the bottlenose dolphin, which is the most common and familiar species[3].

River dolphins are also known as freshwater dolphins and are fully aquatic mammals that live exclusively in freshwater or brackish water[5]. These river dolphins comprise families such as Platanistidae (South Asian dolphins), Lipotidae (possibly extinct Yangtze River dolphin), Iniidae (Amazonian dolphins), and Pontoporiidae[5]. While dolphins are sometimes hunted in areas like Japan and parts of Latin America, they are also kept in captivity for research, conservation, or training in marine mammal parks; the bottlenose dolphin is the most common species kept in captivity[4].

The American Revolution and the French Revolution were ideologically and politically different movements. *   **Political Context:** Political divisions in the U.S. after gaining independence were depicted as less severe compared to the violent polarization between the left and right that began with the French Revolution in 1789[3].

The timeline also shows a progression where the American Revolution's outcome led to political shifts, while the French Revolution marked a more radical societal change starting with the Estates General in 1789 and concluding with the Coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799[1][5].

The French Revolution was a period of political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789 and ended with the Coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799. Many of the revolution's ideas are considered fundamental principles of liberal democracy, and its values remain central to modern French political discourse. It was caused by a combination of social, political, and economic factors which the existing regime proved unable to manage.
Financial crisis and widespread social distress led to the convocation of the Estates General in May 1789, its first meeting since 1614. The representatives of the Third Estate broke away and re-constituted themselves as a National Assembly in June. The Storming of the Bastille in Paris on 14 July led to a series of radical measures by the Assembly, including the abolition of feudalism, state control over the Catholic Church in France, and issuing the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

history.answer: German is the official language of Austria, and it is also considered the lingua franca[3][4]. history.answer: The internet is a global network of computer networks that exchange data using a shared set of rules, the Internet Protocol Suite (TCP/IP). Data is split into small packets, each labeled with the address of its destination. Routers pass the packets from network to network until they reach that address, where they are put back together; packets from one message may take different paths. Every device on the internet has an IP address, and the Domain Name System (DNS) translates names such as wikipedia.org into these addresses. Internet service providers connect homes and businesses, and they are linked by high-capacity backbone cables, including undersea fiber-optic cables. Services such as the World Wide Web and email run on top of this network.

history.answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and some bacteria turn light energy into chemical energy. In plants it takes place mainly in the leaves, inside chloroplasts that contain the green pigment chlorophyll. In the light-dependent reactions, chlorophyll absorbs sunlight, and the energy is used to split water molecules, which releases oxygen and produces the energy carriers ATP and NADPH. In the Calvin cycle, the plant uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide from the air into sugars such as glucose. The overall reaction turns six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water into one molecule of glucose and six of oxygen. Photosynthesis supplies most of the oxygen in the air and the energy for nearly all food chains.

Photosynthesis is how plants, algae, and some bacteria change light energy into the chemical energy they need to live[1]. Essentially, it is a system where these organisms use light energy, usually from the sun, to create the sugars that fuel their metabolism[1][4]. This process involves taking in carbon dioxide and water to manufacture food molecules like starch or cellulose[4].

The core idea is that light energy is used to assemble sugars from carbon dioxide and a source of hydrogen and electrons, which often comes from water[5]. A key part of this process involves a light-dependent reaction where hydrogen gives up its atoms as electrons and protons to carbon dioxide[2]. This reaction releases oxygen as a byproduct when water is split[1]. Some organisms also perform anoxygenic photosynthesis, which does not produce oxygen[3].

top.text: Photosynthesis is a system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria, convert light energy—typically from sunlight—into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism. The term photosynthesis usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, a process that releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting. Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the bonds of intracellular organic compounds (complex compounds containing carbon), typically carbohydrates like sugars (mainly glucose, fructose and sucrose), starches, phytoglycogen and cellulose. When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through cellular respiration. Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the oxygen content of the Earth's atmosphere, and it supplies most of the biological energy necessary for complex life on Earth.

history.query: What caused the fall of the Roman Empire?
history.answer: Historians name many causes for the fall of the Western Roman Empire, which is usually dated to 476, when the last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by Odoacer. Politically, the empire suffered from civil wars, frequent coups and weak emperors, especially during the crisis of the third century. Economically, heavy taxes, inflation from debased coins and shrinking trade weakened it. The army relied more and more on Germanic soldiers and allies whose loyalty was uncertain. From the late fourth century, migrating peoples such as the Goths, Vandals and Huns put pressure on the borders, and the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410. The split of the empire into eastern and western halves also left the poorer West to defend itself, while the Eastern Empire survived until 1453.

history.answer: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape once it passes the boundary called the event horizon. Black holes form when very massive stars collapse at the end of their lives, and supermassive black holes with millions to billions of solar masses sit at the centres of most large galaxies, including the Milky Way. A black hole cannot be seen directly, but astronomers detect it from its effects: the orbits of nearby stars, the glowing disk of hot gas that spirals into it, and gravitational waves when two black holes merge. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87.

history.query: How does a nuclear reactor work?
history.answer: A nuclear reactor produces heat by splitting atoms in a controlled chain reaction. The fuel is usually uranium enriched in uranium-235, formed into pellets and packed into fuel rods. When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it splits into smaller nuclei, releases a large amount of energy as heat, and frees two or three more neutrons that can split other nuclei. A moderator, often water, slows the neutrons so they cause more fissions, and control rods made of neutron-absorbing materials such as boron are moved in or out to keep the reaction steady. The heat boils water, directly or through a heat exchanger, and the steam spins a turbine connected to a generator. Thick shielding and a containment building keep the radiation inside.

answer: A nuclear reactor works by sustaining a controlled chain reaction of nuclear fission to produce heat, which is then used to generate electricity. A nuclear reactor is a device designed to maintain this controlled fission reaction[3]. This process involves stabilizing the reaction by regulating neutron absorbers and moderators within the core[3]. The heat generated from this nuclear fission is transferred to a working fluid coolant[3], and in commercial reactors, this heat drives turbines connected to electrical generator shafts[3].

A nuclear reactor is a device used to sustain a controlled fission nuclear chain reaction. They are used for commercial electricity, marine propulsion, weapons production, and research. Fissile nuclei (primarily uranium-235 or plutonium-239) absorb single neutrons and split, releasing energy and multiple neutrons, which can induce further fission. Reactors stabilize this, regulating neutron absorbers and moderators in the core. Fuel efficiency is exceptionally high; low-enriched uranium is 120,000 times more energy-dense than coal.
Heat from nuclear fission is passed to a working fluid coolant. In commercial reactors, this drives turbines and electrical generator shafts. Some reactors are used for district heating, and isotope production for medical and industrial use.

history.answer: The United Nations is an international organization founded in 1945, after the Second World War, to maintain international peace and security and to promote cooperation between countries. It has 193 member states. Its main bodies include the General Assembly, where every member has a vote, and the Security Council, whose five permanent members, China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, can veto its resolutions. The Secretariat, led by the Secretary-General, runs its daily work, and the International Court of Justice settles disputes between states. Its headquarters are in New York City. Specialized agencies and programmes, such as the World Health Organization and UNICEF, work on health, food, children, refugees and development.

answer:
The United Nations (UN) is an international intergovernmental organization established by the 1945 Charter with the main goal of maintaining international peace and security[1]. It operates through several agencies that form the UN System[1].

Key aspects of the UN include:
*   **Founding and Purpose:** It was established by the signing of the Charter on June 26, 1945, to maintain international peace and security[1][3].
*   **Structure:** The UN System includes principal organs such as the Secretariat, the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice, and the Trusteeship Council[3]. The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA or GA) is one of the six principal organs, serving as its main deliberative, policymaking, and representative body[5].
*   **Focus:** The UN has primarily focused on economic and social development, especially during the mid-twentieth century decolonization period[2].
*   **Operations:** The UN currently operates 11 peacekeeping missions in various regions, including the Middle East, Kashmir, Cyprus, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo[2].
